1:
The opening is remarked on for a curiosity of the text and then for its function. Gill notes that the words to me are wanting in the Hebrew and, as the Masoretic apparatus observes, wanting here alone, though the sense requires them and the Targum supplies them; the desolations at the close of the previous chapter are what this comfort answers. Keil and Delitzsch give the architecture of the whole, that this is the second half of the Lord's answer about the fasts, promising the restitution of the former relation of grace on the simple condition that the moral precepts of the law be observed, and that it divides into two words of God, the first broken into seven sayings and the second into three, each introduced by the same formula; they quote an ancient writer for the reason, that by repeating it the prophet says in effect that promises so incredible in magnitude are not his own but God's. Clarke gives the chapter's outline, the fasts kept during the captivity converted into occasions of rejoicing and the church enlarged by the accession of the Gentiles, with the Jews after their restoration becoming instrumental in converting other nations.

The jealousy in the second verse is where the readings actually part. Calvin reports a view he rejects, that the people are here reproved for unfaithfulness, God comparing himself to a jealous husband whose spouse has violated the marriage; he calls it inadmissible on grammatical grounds, since the verb as construed here with its preposition must be taken in a good sense of concern or affection, as a parallel earlier in the book shows, so that the word means not jealousy but the care God had for his church. Clarke sets out the same options without deciding, that some refer the jealousy to the Jews themselves, punished as an injured husband might punish an unfaithful wife, and others to their enemies, who exceeded their commission and are dealt with in vindictive justice. Wesley holds both halves together, a jealousy of care that she should not sin against his love as before, and a fury against her enemies. Henry reads it as a turning of the same passion, the wrath that had been against her now turned against her adversaries, so that they might promise themselves as much from his anger when it was for them as they had felt when it was against them; and Zion's own sins, he adds, were her worst enemies, so the first act of this jealousy is to take them away. Ellicott corrects only the tense, that both verbs should be present rather than past.

The picture of the restored city is taken literally by everyone and spiritually by one. On the returning, Gill notes the temple was then almost finished and the worship restored, records the Targum's future rendering, and refers the words forward to the incarnation and a later conversion. Ellicott glosses the title city of truth as the place where truth and fidelity towards God have their home, and Wesley as citizens who love the truth and speak it and worship in truth of heart as well as in the manner prescribed. On the old men and women in the streets, Clarke takes it that the followers of God shall live out all their days with the hoary head found in the way of righteousness, while Wesley supplies the contrast, that war and famine and pestilence had formerly cut men off before old age. On the children at play, Gill reads a large increase of inhabitants literally and new-born babes of grace spiritually. Clarke stays with the children and turns the verse into an argument: their gambols are a means of health and a proof of happiness, and since children cannot take exercise except by way of play, such playfulness cannot be sinful, provided they are kept from evil words and scurrility.
6:
The question about what is marvellous is understood by all as a rhetorical one and is put in different words by each. Clarke supplies the objection it answers, that the hearers may think the thing impossible considering their present low condition, and then the retort, that were it impossible in their eyes it need not be so in God's. Ellicott adjusts the tenses, preferring that though it was marvellous in the eyes of the remnant in those days, it will not therefore be marvellous in his; and he sets beside it the saying that what is impossible with men is possible with God. Keil and Delitzsch make the grammar explicit, that the second clause is a question expecting a negative answer, and draw from it a double assurance, of the greatness of the salvation promised and of the certainty that it will be realised. Wesley reduces the whole to a sentence, that these things may seem strange to this people. Gill remarks only that the introductory formula is repeated for confirmation, as a Jewish commentator observes it is at every consolatory promise, and that the following word marks something wonderful and deserving attention.

The gathering from east and west is read by each according to how far he extends it. Wesley keeps it nearest home, taking the east country for the two powers that lay eastward and were then masters of Babylon. Ellicott corrects the impression that only one direction was in question, noting that there were Jews in exile in the west as well as the east and that a very general dispersion may almost be implied by another prophet. Clarke takes the phrase for every land in which any of them may be found, and then says the promises principally regard the Christian church and the bringing in of the Jews with the fulness of the Gentiles. Keil and Delitzsch draw the sharpest distinction: the deliverance did indeed begin with the body of exiles who returned under the first governor, but the deliverance out of all the countries of the earth is still future, the two directions being individualised for all countries; and they argue that this later deliverance is effected through the Messiah, which they take to be indisputable from the promise to bring them to Jerusalem, since the earthly city cannot be meant. Gill reaches the same place by his own route, that the bringing is into the church and the gospel fold, where the other sheep are to be brought so that there may be one fold for Jew and Gentile. On the closing pair of words Wesley divides the responsibility, truth being God's part of the covenant and righteousness theirs, in obedience to his righteous law.
9:
Who is addressed by the call to strong hands is answered by nearly everyone. Gill takes it of those going on with the building of the temple, which he treats as a type of the church. Henry makes the identification the point: the encouragement belongs to those who in obedience to the prophets applied themselves in earnest to the work and were not disobedient as their fathers had been, so the word of consolation is sent to them and not to others; from which he draws the rule that those and only those employed for God may expect encouragement, and that men who avoid their fathers' faults have the entail of a curse turned into a blessing. Wesley names the two prophets meant. Ellicott is less sure, thinking it would almost seem that others spoke at the same time besides those two.

The phrase about the founding of the house draws a chronological argument. Clarke dates it roughly, the founding about two years before this discourse, which fell in the fourth year of the Persian king, and adds that prophets were raised up after it. Ellicott distinguishes two foundations and argues that the resumption is meant rather than the original laying, since the first laying, sixteen years earlier, could hardly be described as done so that the temple might be built when the work was then suspended; and he denies that the old Greek read a different preposition, the Hebrew particle often meaning from the time that.

What the years before were like is described with one instructive difference. Clarke says simply that they had no prosperity but only civil divisions and domestic broils, God having abandoned them to their own spirits and ways. Wesley numbers the period at eighteen years and locates the trouble in the barrenness that made all their labour unprofitable. Ellicott gives the same agricultural cause and adds a political one nobody else mentions, that besides the neighbouring adversaries there fell in that period a Persian expedition against Egypt, whose armies marching south must have distressed a people in narrow circumstances; he records too the old Greek's rendering, turning the past tense into a future by reading the verb as Aramaic. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch mark only the turn that follows, that God will now act differently towards the remnant and bless them again with a fruitful harvest.

The seed that shall be prosperous is where a rendering divides the voices. Clarke and Gill both take the clause plainly, the seed cast in springing up and yielding a large increase where before much sowing came to little. Ellicott prefers the marginal reading, the seed of peace, and identifies it with the vine, which he says is so called because it can flourish only in peaceful times, sitting under one's vine being the common figure for peace and prosperity; he cites the Syriac for the seed shall be peace, and a later historian's description of a people tilling their ground in peace while the earth gave her increase. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same identification by the same reasoning and are careful to reject a different ground for it, that the name comes not from any blessing said to be in the grape but from the vine's dependence on undisturbed times. On the reversal of the curse, Gill applies it to believers reproached by the world as the nation had been by the nations, Clarke promises that they shall be commended instead of reproached and become a blessing to all the nations round, adding that these promises will be completely fulfilled when the Jews acknowledge their Messiah and the restoration is complete in both houses, and Ellicott notes only that the verse is the converse of an older warning.
14:
The ground of the promise is stated as a symmetry, and the voices notice different halves of it. Gill observes that God assures them of what he promises by pointing to the fulfilment of what he threatened, being as faithful in the one as the other. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same structure formally, these verses supplying the ground on which the promise rests and what follows the condition of its fulfilment. Wesley glosses the clause about not repenting as meaning that God did not fail to do what he said, and reads the answering clause as a like steadiness of mind now purposed towards good.

The conditions attached are treated as a short code of civic duty. Gill takes them as obligations incumbent on a people conscious of favours received, to be performed in gratitude. Clarke refers them back to a nearly identical charge in the previous chapter. Ellicott glosses the judgment of truth and peace as one given according to the true facts and tending to peace between man and man, pointing the contrast with a later prophet's complaint of partiality. Wesley locates the gates as the places of judicature where the judges sat. On the prohibition of imagining evil, Gill remarks that hatred without a cause was a governing vice under the second temple, and reports a Jewish commentator's judgment that it caused the temple's destruction.

The answer to the original question about the fasts is identified as such by everybody. Gill says a new prophecy begins here, concerning the abrogation of the fasts and the calling of the Gentiles, and that what follows fully answers the question asked earlier. Keil and Delitzsch describe the last word of God as the direct answer, consisting of three sayings of which the second and third unfold the first. Henry marks who the answer is for: those who fasted in hypocrisy had their doom in the previous chapter, while those who in sincerity humbled themselves and sought God's face receive the assurance of a large share in the coming times.

The four fasts are identified without disagreement, which is unusual in this book. Clarke gives each its occasion: the taking of the city, the ruin of the temple, the murder of the governor, and the beginning of the siege on the tenth day of the tenth month. Wesley names the same occasions and adds the governing condition, that the verse is a final decision of the case provided the duties just required are done, and only then shall the fasting turn into joyful feasts. Ellicott contributes a textual note instead, that the old Greek renders the phrase not as the fast of the fourth month but as the fourth fast, and so with the others. Gill states the promise plainly, that the four are to become joy and gladness and cheerful feasts.

Henry draws the consequences at more length than the rest. He states the rule that joyous times come to the church after troublous ones, and that if weeping endures more than a night and joy does not come next morning, the morning that introduces it will come at length; and he presses the obligation, that when God comes towards us in mercy we must meet him with thankfulness, turning fasts into festivals as he turns judgments into mercies. He also presses the exhortation appended to the promise, that they should love truth and peace: they are to be honest in all their dealings and to find it a pleasure, even where honesty costs them the gains they see others get dishonestly, and to live peaceably with all men, letting the truths of God rule their heads and the peace of God their hearts. He then looks forward to the accession of foreigners promised in the verses following, which he says was fulfilled only in part when proselytes came in during the later days of the Jewish church.
20:
The mutual invitation among the cities is read for its psychology as much as its geography. Gill takes the going of one city's inhabitants to another as evidence of concern for each other's spiritual welfare, of zeal for God's honour, and of readiness to attend divine worship. Clarke fastens on the answering clause and treats it as a reply put into the mouth of the person invited, drawing from it a short exhortation: the work is good, we must have God for a friend, we cannot expect that unless we seek him, and since we do not know what an hour may bring forth we should go speedily. Wesley reduces the whole first verse to a single gloss, that the people spoken of are multitudes. Ellicott, characteristically, records a variant instead: the old Greek makes it the inhabitants of five cities coming together to one, which he supposes borrows the number five from another prophet's promise about five cities in that day. Keil and Delitzsch treat these verses as no new promise at all but as an indication of the nature and magnitude of the salvation already appointed, that by which the fast-days are to be turned into days of joy.

Who the strong nations are is where the voices spread out. Gill takes them for mighty kingdoms, in the Targum's phrase, and points to the professed Christianity of such since the downfall of paganism under Constantine. Clarke looks in a different direction entirely, suggesting the conversion of the Mohammedan tribes, especially those near Palestine, and perhaps also the peoples of Egypt, of the rocky country to the south, and of Syria. Wesley keeps both a literal and a mystical sense, the first-fruits of these nations being the list of peoples present at Pentecost while mystically the city is the church and the praying is all gospel worship. Clarke had already noted that the promise resembles two others in earlier prophets and takes it that many Gentiles as well as Jews will be found devoting themselves to the Lord.

The ten men who seize the skirt draw three treatments of the number and one of the gesture. Ellicott says the number is used indefinitely for a large one, and cites another prophet's use of seven in the same way. Wesley agrees that ten means many, and adds three glosses to the rest: that no nation is any longer excluded, that the man laid hold of is one to whom the gospel was first preached, and that those who speak have now not only heard but seen and are assured, the God in question being the only true God whom to know is life eternal. Clarke offers a proportion first, that the converts from among the Gentiles shall be to the Jews as ten to one, then allows that ten may simply signify a great number without comparison; and he draws the inference the verse invites, that Jews converted to God should be the instruments of converting many Gentiles. On the gesture he observes that catching hold of the skirt is naturally used to entreat assistance and protection. He closes by relaying another scholar's account of what these four verses cover: the accession of converts the Jewish church received between the captivity and the coming of Christ, the number of disciples the Jewish preachers afterwards made, and future conversions of which the restoration of the Jews will be an eminent cause. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same movement more compactly, that the heathen will not merely flow to Jerusalem to seek the God of Israel but will crowd to Israel and Judah to be received into fellowship with them as a nation.
